clue.text: A crude base pounded for condiment

indicators.note: pounded means beaten and broken up, so the letters of the phrase are crushed into a new order

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A rough kitchen base is ground up in a mortar to make a sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pounded' tells you to rearrange the ten letters of A CRUDE BASE. Bread sauce is a British condiment of milk thickened with breadcrumbs, served with roast poultry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread sauce is a classic accompaniment served with roast chicken or turkey, so it is an example of a condiment.

clue.text: Having each time bumped off 50%, sombre hitmen in German city

indicators.note: bumping off half a word means killing its first half, so only the back half of sombre survives

parts.note: losing its first half SOM leaves BRE

indicators.note: each time says the same halving is done again, here to hitmen, keeping only its back half

parts.note: losing its first half HIT leaves MEN

explanation.surface: A gangland thriller: grim contract killers who have rubbed out half their targets in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bumped off' suits the hitmen, but it means cut away: 'Having each time bumped off 50%' halves both sombre and hitmen, keeping BRE and MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Bremen is a port city in northern Germany, capital of the smallest German state.

clue.text: Groups of rowers called out: 'Little islands!'

indicators.note: Calling something out is saying it aloud, so what follows is offered as a noise to be written down some other way.

parts.note: an ait is a small island in a river — the Thames is full of them — and the plural said aloud is spelt quite differently in the grid

explanation.surface: A crew of rowers shouting about the islets they are sweeping past.
explanation.walkthrough: A rowing eight is named by the number of oarsmen in the boat, so the plural means crews rather than numbers, and 'ait' is the old English word for a river islet.
explanation.definitionFit: An eight is a racing shell crewed by eight rowers, so 'groups of rowers' names the crews themselves rather than the boats they sit in.

clue.text: Supply more cured meat: all I ever hoped for

indicators.note: Read as the adverb from 'supple' — SUP-lee, meaning pliantly — it describes letters bending into a new shape, not a delivery of goods.

parts.note: thirteen letters of fodder — M, O, R, E, C, U, R, E, D, M, E, A and T — rearranged

explanation.surface: A butcher being asked for more bacon and ham than anyone could reasonably wish for.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word looks like a verb ordering the meat about, and it is an adverb stressed on its own first syllable: supply, as in supplely.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream come true is the thing you wanted most actually happening, which is what 'all I ever hoped for' says in the first person.

clue.text: Hides vase that's damaged, wanting glue etc

indicators.note: damaged means broken, so the letters of the two words are smashed and put back together differently

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hides a broken vase and goes looking for something to mend it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' tells you to rearrange the letters of HIDES VASE; 'that's' and 'wanting' only link the fodder to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Glue is one kind of sticking agent, and the 'etc' widens it to the whole class of bonding substances.

clue.text: Primarily: cannon — adroit rebound — or miscue?

definitions.text: Primarily: cannon — adroit rebound — or miscue?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, and applied to a list it asks for the letter each item starts with and nothing more.

parts.note: the first letter of the first item on the list
the first letter of the second
the first letter of the third
even the little joining word gives up its opening letter
the first letter of the last item, and the run is printed in order

explanation.surface: A billiards player running through what the shot he has just played might turn out to be.
explanation.walkthrough: A cannon is the British name for the stroke that strikes both other balls, so every item on the list describes one shot — which is what stops the list reading as a list.
explanation.definitionFit: At billiards a carom is a cannon, an adroit rebound off both other balls, so the whole clue describes the shot at the same time as spelling it.

clue.text: Auteur's work, French, in retrospective: '1051'

indicators.note: looking in retrospect means looking back, so the Roman numeral is read backwards

parts.note: in Roman numerals 1051 is M (1000), L (50) and I (1)

explanation.surface: A critic's review of a French director's retrospective season, citing a catalogue number.
explanation.walkthrough: The number is a Roman numeral in disguise; 'in retrospective' sends it backwards before it joins F for French. The quotation marks dress it up as a film title.
explanation.definitionFit: An auteur is a director with a personal style, and what such a director makes is a movie.

clue.text: Affection gleaned from Tin Tim, a cyborg

indicators.note: To glean is to pick up what is already lying in a field, so the letters are gathered from where they sit rather than built.

parts.note: eight consecutive letters run through this phrase, starting one letter into the first word and crossing three word breaks

explanation.surface: A cyborg called Tin Tim, and the warmth somebody manages to get out of him.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd name and the comma make you read 'Tin Tim' as a character being introduced, and a sentence that strains for a name like that is usually straining to hide a run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Intimacy is close personal warmth between people, so 'affection' stands in for it as an everyday synonym — the shared-life sense, not the physical one.

clue.text: Herb's rearranged components to present Tudor ship

indicators.note: the two parts of the herb's name swap places, so the front half moves to the back

parts.note: rosemary is a herb

explanation.surface: Someone shuffles the pieces of a herb's name to reveal a famous vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: ROSEMARY splits into ROSE and MARY; 'rearranged components' swaps those two words round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mary Rose was Henry VIII's flagship, which sank in 1545 and was raised from the Solent in 1982.

clue.text: Bird of prey left in earnest? Not quite

indicators.note: 'In' puts the letter beside it inside the following word rather than in front of it.

parts.note: earnest gives EAGER, and stopping short of the end leaves its R behind
L is the standard short form for left, as on a stage direction or a boot

explanation.surface: A bird of prey abandoned in all seriousness — or not quite all seriousness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the past tense of leave, carrying on the sentence about the bird, and it is a single letter waiting to be dropped inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle is a large hooked-beaked hunting bird, so 'bird of prey' defines it by the class it belongs to rather than by name.

clue.text: Calcium-rich liquid hurtling earthward

indicators.note: Something hurtling is travelling too fast to be controlled, and letters thrown about like that land in an order nobody chose.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder — E, A, R, T, H, W, A, R and D — rearranged

explanation.surface: Rain or hail coming down out of the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'hurtling earthward' as a description of falling rain is the trap; it is an instruction plus the single word it acts on. Hard water is water heavy in dissolved calcium, the kind that furs up a kettle.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard water carries dissolved calcium and magnesium salts picked up from chalk and limestone, so the definition states its chemistry plainly.

clue.text: Question about York and Orleans that's no surprise?

definitions.meaning: both cities wear the same word in front of their names, so the question asks what other things wear it
the weary reply you make when somebody reports something entirely predictable

explanation.surface: A quiz question about two cities, of a kind nobody could find startling.
explanation.walkthrough: New York and New Orleans share their first word, so taken literally the phrase is a genuine question about which other things are new; taken as idiom it is a shrug.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight it asks what else carries the word both cities begin with, and read as idiom it is the sarcastic response to news that surprises nobody.

clue.text: Says goodbye forever to snob met in resort

indicators.note: Read as re-sort rather than as a seaside town, it asks for the letters to be put in order a second time.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder — S, N, O, B, M, E and T — rearranged

explanation.surface: Waving off a stuck-up acquaintance you happened to run into on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' holds the holiday scene together while quietly meaning re-sort, and the definition is a euphemism: saying goodbye forever is burial talk.
explanation.definitionFit: To entomb someone is to seal them in a tomb, the last farewell anybody gets, so the definition names burial without using the word.

clue.text: When reversing, drive into no Shakespearean master somewhere in SE Asia

indicators.note: Reversing sends a vehicle back the way it came, and an across entry taken that way is written out from its right-hand end.

parts.note: to drive into something is to ram it — the phrase works as one instruction, not a verb plus a preposition
nay is the old word for no that fills the plays
M is the standard short form for Master, the title once written on a boy's envelope

explanation.surface: A driver backing into somebody who is no Shakespeare scholar, out in Southeast Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: Myanmar is the country the British called Burma. All three pieces are assembled first and the whole string is turned round at once, which is why no single word looks reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Myanmar is the Southeast Asian state between Bangladesh and Thailand, so the definition places it by region instead of naming anything about it.

clue.text: Perhaps ladies' devices offering comfort

definitions.meaning: the Ladies is the British sign on a women's public lavatory, and 'perhaps' flags it as one instance of a politer general word
the labour-saving household fittings advertised as modern: the washing machine, the dishwasher, the immersion heater

explanation.surface: Gadgets aimed at women, sold on the comfort they promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Ladies' is the sign on a British women's public lavatory, and such a place is a public convenience. The apostrophe is the only clue that a possessive noun is meant rather than an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Public conveniences are British public lavatories, of which the Ladies is one; conveniences are equally the appliances that make a household comfortable.

clue.text: Once called, enjoys fancy meal, initially suppressing desire for attention

parts.note: née is the label for the surname a married woman was born with — what she was once called
to dine is to take a proper sit-down meal rather than merely eat

indicators.note: 'Initially' asks for the very start of the word it introduces, one letter and no more of it.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word the instruction points at

explanation.surface: A woman once known by another name sitting down to a grand dinner and holding her feelings in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Née' introduces a married woman's maiden name, so 'once called' is a standing crossword convention. 'Suppressing' looks like a container instruction and is wanted for its first letter alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Neediness is wanting more notice and reassurance than other people are giving you, which is what 'desire for attention' names outright.

clue.text: Strong drink and some kebabs — in theory

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows rather than all of it, and the part wanted is one unbroken run.

parts.note: eight consecutive letters run through this phrase, starting three letters into the first word and carrying straight on across the dash

explanation.surface: An order of strong drink with a few kebabs, at least in principle.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'in theory' look like a comment on the whole sentence rather than material. Absinthe is the green wormwood spirit banned across Europe for most of the twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Absinthe is a wormwood spirit bottled at up to seventy per cent alcohol, so 'strong drink' names it by the property everyone knows it for.

clue.text: Punishment dispatched: receiver of stolen goods decapitated

parts.note: to dispatch a letter is to send it, so dispatched means sent

indicators.note: decapitated means beheaded, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: a fence is slang for someone who buys and sells stolen goods

explanation.surface: A crime story: the dealer in stolen property was executed by beheading as his punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an execution, but 'decapitated' is about letters, not a head; fence is the old slang for a handler of stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentence is the penalty a court imposes on a convicted person.

clue.text: Terry saw bees, bizarrely, as help in making beer

indicators.note: bizarrely means in an odd, mixed-up way, so the letters of the phrase are jumbled

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Terry oddly spots some bees while helping to brew beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bizarrely' tells you to rearrange the twelve letters of TERRY SAW BEES; 'as' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Brewer's yeast ferments the sugars in wort into alcohol, so it is an essential agent in beer production.

clue.text: Relatively pleasant young Germans

definitions.meaning: 'relatively' asks for the comparative degree — more so than something else — of a word meaning pleasant
the German plural of Kind, meaning children, familiar in English from Kindergarten

explanation.surface: German youngsters being called reasonably agreeable company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relatively' is not the hedge meaning 'fairly' but an instruction to put the adjective into its comparative form, and the second definition is a German word rather than an English one.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinder is the comparative of kind, so 'relatively pleasant' means more pleasant; the same six letters are the German plural for children.

clue.text: Trousers — loud and large — are last thing in grooviness

parts.note: F is forte on a score, the musician's mark for loud
L is the size printed on a clothing label
the clue's own word, lifted out of the sentence and used exactly as it stands

indicators.note: The last thing in a word is the letter it ends on, and only that one letter is being asked for.

parts.note: the final letter of the word that closes the clue

explanation.surface: Trousers described as loud and large, and the very last word in 1970s style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grooviness' is in the clue because these trousers belong to the early 1970s, and 'are' is the one word doing no wordplay job beyond handing over its own three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Flares are trousers that widen sharply from the knee down, so 'trousers' names the garment and leaves out the shape that gives it its name.

clue.text: Detains trainees …

definitions.meaning: the verb, stressed on its second syllable: confining people without charge, as governments do in wartime
the noun, stressed on its first syllable: junior staff learning a trade on the job, especially in American hospitals

explanation.surface: Somebody locking up the new recruits.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the clue on into 23 across so the two read as one sentence, but each half is a complete clue by itself. Verb and noun are spelled alike and stressed differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To intern someone is to hold them in custody without charge, and interns are trainees on placement — one spelling, two unrelated senses.

clue.text: Heavens! Abrupt right for one doing slaloms?

indicators.note: abrupt suggests something cut short, so the last letter of the word for heavens is lopped off

parts.note: the skies are the heavens above

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a sudden sharp right turn, the sort a slalom racer makes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavens!' with its exclamation mark reads as a cry of surprise, but it is the plain noun for the sky above; 'Abrupt' then cuts that word short.
explanation.definitionFit: A slalom is a zigzag downhill race between gates, run by a person on skis.

clue.text: … first sign

definitions.meaning: the adjective: coming before all the others, as in a first attempt
the verb: putting your letters on a document to show it has passed through your hands

explanation.surface: The earliest hint that something is starting to happen.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading ellipsis makes this look like the tail of the previous clue, so the two words read as one phrase about an early symptom when they are separate definitions, an adjective and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Initial means first — an initial attempt — and to initial a document is to sign it with your initials rather than your full name.

clue.text: Argentine mixed fruit

indicators.note: Mixing leaves everything in the bowl in some order other than the one it went in, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder — A, R, G, E, N, T, I, N and E — rearranged

explanation.surface: An Argentinian dish of mixed fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed fruit' reads as one phrase off a menu, which hides the fact that only the first of those two words is doing any mixing and the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangerine is a small loose-skinned citrus, so 'fruit' defines it by its class — the broadest label the setter could have chosen.

clue.text: Deliver a new flipping low

indicators.note: Flipping a thing turns it over end for end, so the letters assembled before it are read out the other way.

parts.note: to rid someone of a burden is to deliver them from it
the clue's own word, taken as the single letter it is
N is the standard short form for new

explanation.surface: Somebody handing over something new and grumbling that it is flipping low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' passes as the mild British swear word attached to 'low', and that is the whole disguise: it is the instruction, and the word it seemed to be modifying is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the point directly beneath you, opposite the zenith, so it serves as the low point of a career, a mood or a season.

clue.text: Lamb's mum runs for source of water

parts.note: a lamb's mother is a female sheep
R stands for runs on a cricket scorecard, the column holding each batter's total

explanation.surface: A mother sheep making a dash for the nearest stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' reads as the verb the sheep is doing, and it is a cricketing abbreviation standing still. A ewer is the tall jug that stood beside a washbasin before plumbing.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a wide-mouthed jug kept on a washstand, so 'source of water' is where the water in the basin came from rather than a spring or a river.

clue.text: Troubles, overwhelming perhaps, foil Everyman's business

indicators.note: To overwhelm something is to come down over the top of it, so the first word closes round the one that follows.
'Perhaps' warns that the word beside it is one example of the thing wanted rather than a synonym for it.

parts.note: to cross somebody is to trouble or thwart them
a foil is the light blunted blade used in fencing, so it is one kind of the weapon wanted

explanation.surface: Overwhelming problems getting in the way of Everyman's line of work.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the pen name of the setter of this puzzle, so the definition is him naming his own trade — and 'foil' is a blade here, not the verb the sentence wants it to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyman sets the Observer's Sunday puzzle, so crosswords are literally his business, and the definition is the setter pointing at himself.
